title: Targeting Host Factors Essential for EBV Episome Persistence
text:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) establishes lifelong infection in humans and is associated with various
diseases, including infectious mononucleosis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and
lymphoproliferative disorders. While the EBV genome is stably maintained within infected cells by
its encoded viral protein EBNA1 and host cellular factors, the host factors involved in this process
remain largely unknown. This study aims to identify these essential host factors, addressing a
critical gap in understanding how EBV hijacks host machinery to sustain lifelong infection and
potentially revealing new therapeutic targets for EBV-associated diseases.

title: Linking Variants to Multi-scale Phenotypes via a Synthesis of Subnetwork Inference and Deep Learning
text:
Being able to characterize the impact of genetic variants on phenotypes is critical for interpreting the roles
these variants play in human health and disease. The proposed research will significantly advance our ability
to predict the impact of genetic variants thereby boosting the effectiveness of genomic analyses ranging from
genome-wide association studies for common diseases to diagnostic odysseys searching for genetic causes of
rare diseases.

title: Structural Biology & Biophysics Core (SBB)
text: Structural Biology and Biophysical (SBB) Core The Structural Biology & Biophysics (SBB) Core of the Indiana University School of Medicine Purdue University TaRget Enablement to Accelerate Therapy Development for Alzheimer's Disease (IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD) Center will help develop high quality lead compounds for novel Alzheimer's Disease (AD) targets. The SBB Core will work in concert with the other Technical Cores to select, produce, characterize, and structurally enable AD targets in support of structure-based drug design for lead optimization. The SBB Core will utilize a two-pronged approach to support the overall goals of the TREAT-AD center. The SBB Core will first characterize the biochemical and biophysical properties of target proteins in the unbound and ligand-bound forms to better understand the kinetics and thermodynamics of ligand engagement with the target. Enzyme kinetic studies, including the use of advanced Desorption Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry (DESI-MS) assays, will be used to determine steady-state kinetic parameters for substrates and ligands. Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR) will be used to determine ligand-binding kinetics and Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) and MicroScale Thermophoresis (MST) will be used to determine ligand-binding thermodynamics. Mass Photometry (MP) and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) with Multi-Angle Light Scattering (MALS) will be used to determine protein quaternary structure and the influence of ligand binding on oligomeric state. Second, the SBB core will work to determine the structures for prioritized targets via X-ray diffraction and/or cryo-electron microscopy. The SBB core will develop approaches and integrated workflow in close collaboration with the MCCB and ADHTS cores for each target protein to acquire data in support SAR analysis and structure-based drug design. The SBB core will also help establish connectivity between molecular design and biological function to enhance understanding of the role of the target proteins in AD processes. The SBB core will work to accomplish these goals and those of the IUSM-Purdue TREAT-AD center through the following Specific Aims: 1) Evaluate the feasibility of nominated protein targets for structure-based design studies, 2) Produce and characterize the biochemical, biophysical, and structural properties of target proteins. 3) Elucidate target structures to guide drug discovery activities.

title: Dissecting enhancer function through integrative genomics
text:
Enhancers are non-coding regulatory elements modulating gene transcription in human diseases. We will
develop computational methods to dissect enhancer function through data integration and machine learning of
eight epigenomic features across hundreds of human cell types. The findings will fill up missing enhancer profiles
and generate tools to prioritize enhancers’ impacts in human diseases.

title: Statistical tensor regression models for intracranial aneurysm growth prediction
text:
The proposed research aims to develop a comprehensive statistical and computational framework to predict the
growth of unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIA) growth at the 24th month as well as their growth trajecto-
ries over a period of ﬁve years. Successful completion of the proposed research will provide a comprehensive
computational system that will serve as a decision support tool for physicians managing patients with UIA. This
information will also help physicians to assess the rupture risk of intracranial aneurysms, and to develop an
appropriate plan for longitudinal surveillance based on the unique hemodynamics of a particular patient's UIA.

title: Project 1: Temporal sequencing in plasma and PET that presage the 'caTAUstrophe'
text: Project 1 - Timing the CaTAUstrophe. Recent findings from anti-Amyloid-β (Aβ) trials in early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease (AD) have demonstrated the value of therapeutic intervention initiated before the rapid spread of neocortical tauopathy (“caTAUstrophe”) that heralds cognitive impairment. Our work using PET imaging in HABS was among the first to demonstrate that rapid neocortical Tau proliferation generally occurs only after Aβ is elevated in preclinical AD. Individual variability in the onset of neocortical Tau accumulation makes it challenging to identify individuals who are at imminent risk for rapid neocortical Tau proliferation. Further work to understand the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of Tau in aging and its relationship with Aβ in the transition to AD is needed to improve screening for current trials and provide a foundation for prevention trials to shift even earlier. We began Tau PET imaging in HABS at the end of the first Cycle with Flortaucipir (FTP), giving us one of the most expansive longitudinal Tau datasets in existence. In the current Cycle, we introduced an Advanced Imaging Cohort (AIC) who have undergone a more intense Tau-PET imaging program with the 18F-MK6240 tracer. Over the next five years, we propose to push the boundaries further by rolling out MK6240 to the entire HABS cohort and pilot testing a state-of-the-art PET/CT tomograph to dive deep into early tauopathy in vivo with more fine- grained anatomical detail than has ever been possible before (see Imaging Core). The overarching goal of Project 1 is to leverage breakthroughs in PET sensitivity and spatial resolution along with recent advances in plasma biomarker assays to go earlier into the spatiotemporal dynamics of Aβ and Tau pathology at the earliest detectable pathological stages of AD. Aim 1 will leverage up to 15 years of previously collected imaging and plasma samples in combination with prospective data acquired with innovative new technologies and methods to examine the joint spatiotemporal trajectories of Aβ and Tau pathologies and improve the prediction of early neocortical Tau accumulation. Aim 2 will focus on the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of MTL Tau in aging and its relationship with Aβ in the transition to AD. Finally, in Aim 3, we will move even earlier in the pathophysiological process to explore the contributions of locus coeruleus (LC) integrity and function to the vulnerability of the MTL region by combining ultra-high field MRI/fMRI (7T) with norepinephrine transporter PET (NET-PET, 11C-MeNER) imaging. Project 1 will contribute to the overall Program goals by providing optimized measures of Aβ and Tau, while collaborating directly with Project 2 to assess the contributions of vascular injury and immune dysregulation to neocortical Tau, with Project 3 to understand cognitive resilience in the face of Aβ and Tau pathology, and with Project 4 using digital tools to enhance detection of the cognitive and functional consequences of emerging pathology.

title: Integrative Omics Facility Core
text: The Omics Facility Core (OFC) assists members in fulfilling the mission of SWEHSC to understand the mechanisms underlying environmental health science (EHS) risks and disease among people living in arid environments by providing high-quality, cost-efficient access to knowledgeable scientists and a full spectrum of modern technologies and techniques. The technologies and techniques within the OFC are used to measure environmental toxicants (exposomics) and their effects on the proteome, metabolome, epigenome, and genome of exposed populations and laboratory models. The OFC is composed of three labs: 1) an exposomic lab providing services to quantitate organic and inorganic toxicants of relevance from diverse matrices such as water, air, dust, bodily tissues, and plants; 2) the proteomics lab providing protein identification, mapping posttranslational modifications, disulfide linkage characterization, peptide sequencing, and biomarker quantitation; and 3) a genomics lab providing next-gen DNA sequencing of whole genomes, exomes, and transcriptomes (RNA-seq), real time RT-PCR, genotyping, fragment analysis, and Sanger sequencing. Finally, epigenomic and metabolomic services including analysis of histone protein modifications, DNA methylation, and quantitation of toxicant metabolites are distributed across the three Omics laboratories based on the analyte and expertise required. The OFC provides Center investigators with prioritized access to state-of-the-art equipment and approaches to achieve the environmental health science (EHS) goals of the SWEHSC. The three Co-Directors of the OFC component labs guide the choice of appropriate analysis, consult on experimental design, manage the analyses and related budget, provide logistical support, provide data interpretation and insight into results, and assist with dissemination of results. Further, the OFC provides training and education to Center investigators’ staff and students to 1) provide access to modern analytic techniques, 2) consult in experimental design and efficient use of resources, 3) ensure services are current through technique development and new equipment acquisition, 4) provide data analysis and interpretation, and 5) assist in the preparation of manuscripts and grant applications. Integration with other SWEHSC resources facilitates the acquisition of omics-level data and information that are necessary to fully determine the sites and modes of toxicant action.

title: Examining nicotine relapse in the habenulo-interpeduncular system
text:
Addiction to tobacco products is exceedingly common in the United States, and nicotine withdrawal and
subsequent relapse is a significant contributor to the addiction process. The goal of this project is to leverage our
well-qualified research team, our innovative tools, and our incisive methods to identify mechanisms that support
tobacco addiction. By identifying these mechanisms, our project will promote the development of new and more
effective strategies to help people quit smoking.

title: Synaptic function of BK channel-interacting proteins
text:
This project is to investigate how melatonin regulates synaptic transmission and sleep through the BK
channel, and how the BK channel is regulated by a newly identified molecular pathway. The results of this
project will help our understanding about the molecular mechanisms of BK channel regulation and of
melatonin’s sleep-promoting effects.

title: Identifying disparities in air pollution-attributable cardiovascular health outcomes within a quasi-experimental framework
text:
The overarching goal of this K01 Career Development Award is to foster Dr. Andrea Titus’s transition to
independence as a social epidemiologist with expertise in examining environmental drivers of cardiovascular
disease disparities. The proposed study will draw on multi-level statistical and machine learning approaches to
investigate associations between fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and disparities across a range of
cardiovascular disease outcomes, leveraging electronic health record data from a national cohort of U.S.
veterans. Findings from this work will contribute to the evidence base regarding the pathogenesis of air
pollution-attributable cardiovascular outcomes and will shed light on potential population subgroups that may
benefit most from targeted interventions to reduce and mitigate air pollution exposures.

title: Low Dose Multivalent Influenza Vaccine via Modified Self-Amplifying RNA
text:
Seasonal influenza remains a significant US health threat, and current egg-based, cell-culture, and RNA vaccine
platforms face substantial limitations such as slow production, high doses, significant side effects, and short-
lived immunity. We propose a novel modified self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine that leverages a catalytic
RNA and modified nucleotides to enable rapid production, substantially lower dosing, reduced side effects, and
durable immune responses of a multi-valent vaccine. Our innovative saRNA platform transforms influenza
vaccination by achieving superior efficacy, improved safety, and faster pandemic response capabilities.

title: Mining Social Media for Barriers and Facilitators to PrEP Uptake and Persistence
text:
A major barrier to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) uptake and persistence in the United States (US) is the
uncertainty regarding PrEP (e.g., uncertainties regarding costs, side effects, details of the drug regimen),
among the general public, many of whom turn to the Internet for information about it—thus, their online posts
and discussions provide insights into the public’s knowledge gaps regarding PrEP. To understand people’s
inquiries and concerns about PrEP and ensure that guidelines and health communication directly address
those uncertainties, this proposal outlines an innovative, community-driven natural language processing (NLP)
analysis in which the trainee will collaborate with the Center for AIDS Research Community Liaison Council, a
diverse group of community members living in the Southeast, the region with the highest HIV prevalence, to
examine a decade’s worth of data from Reddit and Google and (1) assess the public’s knowledge gaps as well
as the barriers and facilitators to PrEP uptake and persistence at the population level and (2) compare the
results of the community-driven NLP analysis with the CDC 2021 PrEP Clinical Practice Guidelines to identify
consistencies and discrepancies between the language laypeople use when discussing PrEP and the
information they seek versus the information provided in the guidelines. This proposal is a step toward tackling
the widespread uncertainty regarding PrEP and will result in (A) community-built PrEP-related lexicon, a
compilation of terms that the general public uses to refer to PrEP and common search queries; (B) an
understanding of PrEP related knowledge gaps, barriers, and facilitators to uptake and persistence at the
population level; and (C) inform community-driven PrEP information dissemination.

title: Combining protein and DNA engineering to create bioswitches
text:
This project seeks to develop proteins and enzymes that are switched on and off by binding of specific DNA or
RNA sequences, as well as by proteins and small molecules. These protein switches will be used as
biosensors for detecting pathogens and disease markers, and to selectively kill virally-infected cells while
leaving uninfected cells unharmed.

title: Roles of DNA and Histone Methylation in Transposon Silencing, High-Temperature Growth, and Genome Stability in Cryptococcus neoformans
text:
Cryptococcus neoformans is a WHO-designated critical priority fungal pathogen responsible for
approximately 194,000 annual cases of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, a disease with a
mortality rate of ~60% and limited treatment options. Central to Cryptococcus pathogenesis is the
ability to adapt to host-relevant stress conditions, including exposure to antifungals and high
temperatures. This study will investigate the roles of DNA and histone H3 methylation in silencing
mutagenic transposable elements and facilitating growth and genome stability at elevated
temperatures, providing essential insights into the epigenetic mechanisms that govern adaptation
to a host-like environment and the virulence of this globally distributed fungal pathogen.

title: National Center for Quantitative Biology of Complex Systems
text:
The National Center for Quantitative Biology of Complex Systems (NCQBCS)
develops, refines, and disseminates quantitative technologies for the analysis of proteins, lipids, and metabolites.
These essential technologies are honed in the context of pressing biomedical problems broad in scientific scope
and efficiently brought out of the Center through a robust community engagement platform and
commercialization. The synergy across these activities ensures that the NCQBCS will fulfill its most critical
mission: to empower all biomedical researchers to maximize biological insight through widespread access to
enabling, sustainable technologies.

title: Combining Laboratory and Ecological Momentary Assessment-based Methods to Determine Age-related Differences in the Relationship Between Alcohol Use, Pain, and Inflammation
text:
Pain and problematic alcohol use each cost hundreds of billions of dollars annually, are attributed to
increased mortality, and co-occur at high rates. Evidence across the literature suggests important age-related
differences in how pain is associated with alcohol use, but age has generally been overlooked with regard to
pain-related alcohol use. By combining data from laboratory-based pain-induction tasks and brief smartphone-
based surveys, this project will examine mechanisms and age-related differences underlying pain-related
alcohol use.

title: Development of an intelligent droplet acoustofluidic platform for automated liquid-liquid handing and monitoring in biomedical research
text:
The proposed project contributes to the development of automated technologies for liquid handling and
monitoring across various fields of chemistry, biology, and medicine. Successful development of this intelligent
droplet acoustofluidic platform may revolutionize current high throughput applications, including sequencing
library preparation, clinical diagnostics, large-scale compound screening, and high-throughput chemical
reactions.

title: Virus breathing and assembly-disassembly transitions in host-entry
text:
Project Title: Virus breathing and assembly–disassembly transitions in host entry
Project Narrative
The critical first steps in an infectious virus’ lifecycle which include receptor recognition and disassembly upon
contact, are poorly understood. Our proposed research program will determine the steps for how intact virus
particles precisely disassemble upon interactions with host cell receptors, to release the viral genome inside the
human host cell. This will be achieved by monitoring virus dynamics in multiple icosahedral model viruses
through integrative structural mass spectrometry, cryo-electron microscopy, biophysical and RNA chemistry
approaches.

title: T cell response in Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans-associated periodontal disease
text:
Periodontitis is a prevalent chronic inflammatory disease that affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide.
This project will determine the immunopathologic consequences of T cell recognition and response to antigen
from a known periodontal pathogen, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans.

title: Alterations to adipose tissue regulation and function by cART in SIV-infected rhesus macaques
text:
The proposed project will investigate how SIV and cART-mediated dysfunction in adipose tissue and adipose
stem cells (ASCs) contributes to increased obesity in people living with HIV (PLWH). The research will
specifically examine how SIV, cART, and their combination alter the function and differentiation of adipocytes
and ASCs. This study is crucial for elucidating the specific role of cART drugs on adipose tissue, an essential
site for HIV-related health issues.
